## Research questions and data

This project extends DATASCI 306 Homework 5 by asking how hurricane activity varies **by year, season, intensity, and location**, and by comparing several statistical approaches to wind speed and central pressure. The `storms.csv` file contains repeated time-stamped observations; treating them as separate independent storms would inflate counts and overstate precision.

```{r load-and-analysis, results='hide', fig.show='hide'}
# Reproduce all calculations and save the six figures.
source("hurricane_analysis.R", local = knitr::knit_global())
```

## Data validation and missingness

```{r data-audit}
print(dim(storms))
print(missing_counts)
```

The category variable is naturally missing in many records of non-hurricane systems; the wind and pressure fields used here do not require imputation. We distinguish **655 storm-year groups** from **319 storms observed at hurricane strength**.

## Annual hurricane counts

The custom `annual_hurricane_counts()` function counts each distinct `(year, name)` pair only once, even if the same storm has dozens of measurements.

```{r annual-counts}
print(head(yearly))
print(p1)
```

## Seasonality: month of first hurricane classification

This counts each hurricane in the **first month it was observed with hurricane status**; it is not the same as storm genesis or the number of recorded observations per month.

```{r seasonality}
print(monthly_hurricanes)
print(p3)
```

## Annual intensity changes

We select one peak-wind hurricane-stage record per named storm and summarize its wind speed by year. The fitted trend is descriptive: observation changes and natural variability prevent a simple climate-causation interpretation.

```{r intensity-trends}
print(head(annual_intensity))
print(coef(summary(intensity_trend)))
print(p4)
```

## Wind versus pressure: Pearson, Spearman, OLS

The first two correlations assess different patterns. **Pearson** measures linear association; **Spearman** measures monotonic rank association. The fitted ordinary least-squares regression summarizes the average change in pressure with wind speed, without claiming a causal relationship.

```{r association}
cat("Pearson r:", unname(pearson_result$estimate), "\n")
cat("Spearman rho:", unname(spearman_result$estimate), "\n")
print(coef(summary(pressure_model)))
cat("R squared:", summary(pressure_model)$r.squared, "\n")
print(p2)
```

## Chi-squared test on quantile groups

The `to_tercile()` function creates wind and pressure classes from their 1/3 and 2/3 quantiles, then a chi-squared test examines their association. The variables were originally continuous; this grouping sacrifices information and is presented as a complementary exercise, not a replacement for correlation/regression.

```{r chi-squared}
print(frequency)
print(chi)
cat("Minimum expected cell count:", min(chi$expected), "\n")
```

## Category comparison and geographic patterns

We compare **pressure across hurricane wind-based categories**, rather than treating category and wind speed as independent characteristics. The spatial display uses **one peak-intensity location per hurricane** rather than all observations, which would overrepresent longer-lived storms.

```{r categories}
print(p5)
```

```{r spatial}
print(p6)
```

## Interpretation and limitations

- Seasonal counts represent the first **hurricane-status** month, not the formation month.
- Data points in wind-pressure analysis represent distinct `(year, name)` pairs, using a maximum-wind record; the choice of record affects the estimates.
- The OLS model is descriptive, not causal; linear-model assumptions should be checked before using it for formal prediction.
- Changes in detection/reporting practices and large year-to-year variability complicate long-run trend claims.
- Coordinates mark locations at peak recorded intensity, not hurricane origin or landfall.

**Data source:** `storms.csv` from the `dplyr` v1.1.4 data repository. **Provenance:** Adapted and extended from DATASCI 306 HW5.
